A.q: The simple present describes:
A.explain: The simple present describes habits, general truths, feelings or thoughts.
options: Habits, general truths, feelings or thoughts
Actions that happened in the past
Actions that will happen in the future

A.q: Which sentence is in the simple present tense?
A.explain: 'She loves to shop online' expresses a feeling/thought in the simple present.

A.q: Which of the following is NOT described by the simple present tense?
A.explain: Actions in progress at this moment are described by the present continuous, not the simple present.
options: Actions in progress at this moment

A.q: 'People spend lots of money.' This sentence expresses:
A.explain: This is a general truth about people's behavior.

A.q: 'John eats green apples.' This sentence expresses:
A.explain: Eating green apples is a habit/routine for John.

A.q: What is the pronunciation of the -s in 'visits'?
A.explain: Visit ends in /t/ (voiceless), so -s is pronounced /s/.

A.q: What is the pronunciation of the -s in 'takes'?
A.explain: Take ends in /k/ (voiceless), so -s is pronounced /s/.

A.q: What is the pronunciation of the -s in 'laughs'?
A.explain: Laugh ends in /f/ (voiceless), so -s is pronounced /s/.

A.q: What is the pronunciation of the -s in 'reads'?
A.explain: Read ends in a voiced sound /d/, so -s is pronounced /z/.

A.q: What is the pronunciation of the -s in 'plays'?
A.explain: Play ends in a vowel sound, so -s is pronounced /z/.

A.q: Which verb has the -s pronounced as /iz/?
A.explain: Watch ends in -ch, so -es is pronounced /iz/.

A.q: Which verb has the -s pronounced as /s/?
A.explain: Take ends in /k/ (voiceless), so -s is pronounced /s/.

A.q: What is the correct structure for an information question in the simple present?
A.explain: Information questions follow: Wh-word + Do/Does + Subject + Base Verb.

A.q: What is the correct structure for a yes/no question in the simple present?
A.explain: Yes/No questions follow: Do/Does + Subject + Base Verb.

A.q: Which verb is NOT typically used for feelings and emotions in the simple present?
A.explain: 'Run' is an action verb, not a feeling/emotion verb.

A.q: Which sentence expresses a feeling or emotion?
A.explain: 'Feels afraid' expresses an emotion.
options: The sun rises in the morning.

A.q: Which sentence expresses a fact or general truth?
A.explain: The sun rising in the morning is a general truth/fact.
options: I play games online every night.
The sun rises in the morning.

A.q: Which sentence expresses a general truth?
A.explain: Water freezing at 0 degrees is a scientific fact/general truth.

A.q: What is the basic English sentence structure?
A.explain: The basic English sentence structure is Subject + Verb.

A.q: Which word has the correct -s pronunciation?
A.explain: Watches = /iz/. Sleeps = /s/, plays = /z/, reads = /z/.

A.q: ___ your teacher speak German?
A.explain: Your teacher is third-person singular, so question uses Does + base verb speak.

A.q: He ___ do karate.
A.explain: Negative with he uses doesn't + base verb do. The main verb remains do.

A.q: Susan ___ learn Spanish at school.
A.explain: Susan is third-person singular, so negative uses doesn't + base verb learn.

A.q: Which correlation is correct for Present Simple?
A.explain: Plural and I/you subjects use do. Third-person singular uses does.

A.q: Which correlation is correct for frequency adverbs?
A.explain: I am never late. / I never go late.
options: With be → after be; with other verbs → before the main verb
With be → before be; with other verbs → after the main verb
Always at the end of the sentence
Always at the beginning of the sentence

A.q: Which correlation is correct for time prepositions?
A.explain: at seven o'clock, in the morning, on Saturdays.
options: at + clock time; in + morning/afternoon/evening; on + days/dates
at + days; in + clock time; on + morning
in + clock time; at + months; on + years
on + clock time; at + days; in + dates

A.q: Choose the correct sentence.
A.explain: After doesn't, the main verb is base form do. He takes doesn't, not don't.

A.q: Choose the correct sentence.
A.explain: After doesn't, use base verb spend, not spends.
options: She doesn't spend her free time with her friends.
She doesn't spends her free time with her friends.
She don't spend her free time with her friends.
She not spend her free time with her friends.

A.q: Choose the correct question.
A.explain: After Does, use base verb work.
options: Does her mother work in the bank?
Does her mother works in the bank?
Do her mother work in the bank?
Does her mother working in the bank?

A.q: Which sentence correctly uses the article and frequency expression?
A.explain: Use the swimming pool and twice a week. He takes goes.
options: He goes to the swimming pool twice a week.
He goes to swimming pool twice a week.
He goes to the swimming pool two times week.
He go to the swimming pool twice a week.

A.q: Which sentence is correct?
A.explain: Leave for work means depart to go to work. Use do with you.
options: What time do you leave for work?
What time you do leave for work?
What time do you leave work for?
What time does you leave for work?

A.q: Which sentence is correct?
A.explain: Use do with you. Possessive your comes before room.
options: How often do you clean your room?
How often you clean your room?
How often does you clean your room?
How often do you clean room your?

A.q: Which correlation is correct for negative Present Simple?
A.explain: After don't/doesn't, the main verb does not take -s: He doesn't go, not He doesn't goes.

A.q: Which correlation is correct for be in Present Simple?
A.explain: I am, he/she/it is, you/we/they are.
options: I → am; he/she/it → is; you/we/they → are
I → is; he/she/it → am; you/we/they → are
I → are; he/she/it → is; you/we/they → am

A.q: Which sentence correctly uses a frequency adverb with be?
A.explain: With be, frequency adverbs go after the verb: am never.
options: I am never late for school.
I never am late for school.
I am late never for school.
I never be late for school.

A.q: Which sentence correctly uses seldom?
A.explain: Seldom goes before the main verb. We takes have.
options: We seldom have lunch at noon.
We have seldom lunch at noon.
We seldom has lunch at noon.
Seldom we have lunch at noon.

A.q: Which sentence is correct?
A.explain: Use was born for past birth and in + year.

A.q: Which sentence is correct?
A.explain: Both Mandy and she are third-person singular: finishes, meets.
options: Mandy finishes work at 2 o'clock and sometimes she meets friends for lunch.
Mandy finish work at 2 o'clock and sometimes she meet friends for lunch.
Mandy finishes work at 2 o'clock and sometimes she meet friends for lunch.
Mandy finish work at 2 o'clock and sometimes she meets friends for lunch.

A.q: Which sentence is correct?
A.explain: Third-person singular negative uses does not + base verb have.
options: Michael does not have any brothers or sisters.
Michael do not have any brothers or sisters.
Michael not has any brothers or sisters.
Michael doesn't has any brothers or sisters.

A.q: Which sentence is correct?
A.explain: The other waiters and they are plural, so arrive and tidy are base forms.
options: The other waiters arrive at seven o'clock and they tidy the kitchen.
The other waiters arrives at seven o'clock and they tidies the kitchen.
The other waiters arrive at seven o'clock and they tidies the kitchen.
The other waiters arrives at seven o'clock and they tidy the kitchen.

A.q: Which sentence is correct?
A.explain: Both verbs describe he, so both take -s: loves, wants.
options: He loves basketball and wants to be a professional basketball player.
He love basketball and want to be a professional basketball player.
He loves basketball and want to be a professional basketball player.
He love basketball and wants to be a professional basketball player.

A.q: Which sentence is correct?
A.explain: Both loves and enjoys are third-person singular forms.
options: In his free time, Michael loves playing computer games and he enjoys watching TV.
In his free time, Michael love playing computer games and he enjoy watching TV.
In his free time, Michael loves playing computer games and he enjoy watching TV.
In his free time, Michael love playing computer games and he enjoys watching TV.

A.q: But we ___ there now.
A.explain: With 'we', use 'don't' + base verb.

A.q: We ___ in Houston with our two children.
A.explain: With 'we', use the base verb 'live'.

A.q: Fernanda's parents ___ with us in Texas.
A.explain: 'Parents' is plural, and the verb is 'be', so use 'aren't'.

A.q: Fernanda ___ in touch with them online.
A.explain: Fernanda is third-person singular, so add -s: stays.

A.q: Every day, she ___ by e-mail with her parents.
A.explain: She is third-person singular, so use 'communicates'.

A.q: She ___ them a lot of pictures of their grandchildren.
A.explain: She is third-person singular, so use 'sends'.

A.q: We ___ back home very often.
A.explain: With 'we', use 'don't' + base verb.

A.q: Because plane tickets ___ expensive.
A.explain: 'Plane tickets' is plural, so use 'are'.

A.q: Fernanda's parents ___ to Houston often.
A.explain: With plural 'parents', use 'don't' + base verb.

A.q: As a result, Fernanda rarely ___ them.
A.explain: Fernanda is third-person singular, so use 'sees'.

A.q: I rarely ___ my parents, either.
A.explain: With 'I', use the base verb 'see'.

A.q: Fernanda and I ___ our families and friends in Guatemala a lot.
A.explain: With the plural compound subject 'Fernanda and I', use the base verb 'miss'.

A.q: Fernanda rarely sees them. 'Rarely' means ___.
A.explain: 'Rarely' means not often. 'Never' is stronger.

A.q: I rarely see my parents, ___.
A.explain: 'Either' is used to agree with a negative statement.

A.q: My family and friends ___ the computer for all sorts of things.
A.explain: The compound subject is plural, so the base verb 'use' is correct.

A.q: My friend Mark ___ for clothes online.
A.explain: Third-person singular takes -s: shops.

A.q: Our classmates Marta and Raul ___ their email at the library.
A.explain:
Marta and Raul is a plural subject, so use 'check'.
"email" vs "e-mail", email (without the hyphen) is the modern standard used in almost all professional, academic, and everyday writing today.

A.q: My best friend Ana ___ on any social networking sites.
A.explain: The verb 'be' is negated with 'isn't' for a singular subject.

A.q: Ana and her sister Claudia ___ groceries online.
A.explain: Ana and Claudia is a plural subject, so use 'don't buy'.

A.q: My family ___ a lot of time online.
A.explain: 'My family' is treated as a singular unit here, so use 'spends'.

A.q: My brother Sam is online a lot, but he also ___ with our family.
A.explain: He is third-person singular, so use 'interacts'.

A.q: Technology ___ my relationships.
A.explain: Technology is singular, so use 'doesn't' + base verb 'hurt'.

A.q: Which is the correct Yes/No question for: I use an online dictionary for my classes.
A.explain: With 'I' in a question to someone, use 'Do you' and change 'my' to 'your'.
options: Do you use an online dictionary for your classes?
Does you use an online dictionary for your classes?
Do I uses an online dictionary for my classes?
Are you use an online dictionary for your classes?

A.q: Which is the correct Yes/No question for: Our classmates Marta and Raul check their e-mail at the library.
A.explain: Marta and Raul is plural, so use 'Do' + base verb 'check'.
options: Do your classmates Marta and Raul check their e-mail at the library?
Does your classmates Marta and Raul check their e-mail at the library?
Do your classmates Marta and Raul checks their e-mail at the library?
Are your classmates Marta and Raul check their e-mail at the library?

A.q: Which is the correct Yes/No question for: My best friend Ana isn't on any social networking sites.
A.explain: To make a neutral Yes/No question from a negative 'be' sentence, put 'Is' first.
options: Is your best friend Ana on any social networking sites?
Does your best friend Ana be on any social networking sites?
Isn't your best friend Ana on any social networking sites?
Do your best friend Ana is on any social networking sites?

A.q: Which is the correct Yes/No question for: Ana and her sister Claudia don't buy groceries online.
A.explain: The subject is plural, and the neutral question removes 'don't' and uses 'Do'.
options: Do Ana and her sister Claudia buy groceries online?
Does Ana and her sister Claudia buy groceries online?
Don't Ana and her sister Claudia buy groceries online?
Are Ana and her sister Claudia buy groceries online?

A.q: Which is the correct Yes/No question for: My family spends a lot of time online.
A.explain: Family is singular here, so use 'Does' + base verb 'spend'.
options: Does your family spend a lot of time online?
Do your family spend a lot of time online?
Does your family spends a lot of time online?
Is your family spend a lot of time online?

A.q: Which is the correct Yes/No question for: My brother Sam interacts with our family.
A.explain: Sam is singular, so use 'Does' + base verb 'interact'; 'my/our' changes to 'your' in the question.
options: Does your brother Sam interact with your family?
Do your brother Sam interact with your family?
Does your brother Sam interacts with your family?
Is your brother Sam interact with your family?

A.q: Which is the correct Yes/No question for: Technology doesn't hurt my relationships.
A.explain: Technology is singular, so use 'Does' + base verb 'hurt'.

A.q: Which is the correct Wh-question for: My friend Mark shops for clothes online. Ask about place.
A.explain: Mark is singular, so use 'does' + base verb 'shop'.
options: Where does your friend Mark shop for clothes?
Does your friend Mark shop for clothes online?
Where does your friend Mark shops for clothes?
Where your friend Mark shops for clothes?

A.q: Which is the correct Wh-question for: My family spends a lot of time online. Ask about amount.
A.explain: Family is singular, so use 'does' + base verb 'spend'.
options: How much time does your family spend online?
How much time do your family spend online?
How much time does your family spends online?
How much time your family spends online?

A.q: Which is the correct Wh-question for: My brother Sam interacts with our family. Ask about person.
A.explain: Sam is singular, so use 'does' + base verb 'interact'.
options: Who does your brother Sam interact with?
Who does your brother Sam interacts with?
Who do your brother Sam interact with?
Who your brother Sam interacts with?

A.q: Which subject takes 'is'?
A.explain: Fernanda is singular.

A.q: Which subject takes 'spends'?
A.explain: My family is singular here.

A.q: Which subject takes 'isn't'?
A.explain: Ana is singular and uses 'be'.

A.q: Which subject takes 'aren't'?
A.explain: Parents is plural and uses 'be'.

A.q: Which is correct?
A.explain: The plural of child is children.

A.q: Which is correct?
A.explain: Plane tickets is plural, so use 'are'.

A.q: Which is correct?
A.explain: Technology is singular, so use 'doesn't' + base verb 'hurt'.

A.q: Every day signals ___.
A.explain: Every day is a common simple present time expression.

A.q: Which is the correct spelling of the term for keeping in contact via the internet?
A.explain: The correct spelling is 'online' (one word).

A.q: Which is plural?
A.explain: Families is the plural form.

A.q: Which is plural?
A.explain: Friends is the plural form.

A.q: Which sentence is wrong?
A.explain: After 'does', use the base verb 'spend', not 'spends'.
options: Does your family spends a lot of time online?
Does your family spend a lot of time online?
Do your family and friends use the computer?

A.q: Which of the following sentences is written in the simple present tense?
A.explain: The verb 'improve' is in its base form, indicating a general fact or truth, which is the primary use of the simple present tense.
options: Chemicals in blueberries improve your brain.
They are all improving their brains.

A.q: Which sentence best describes a general truth using the simple present tense?
A.explain: General truths and scientific facts are expressed using the simple present tense, as seen with the verb 'helps'.
options: Exercise helps the brain, not just the body.
Anthony is jogging in the park.

A.q: What is the 3rd person singular form of the verb 'like'?
A.explain: Most verbs simply add -s in the 3rd person singular.

A.q: What is the 3rd person singular form of the verb 'hiss'?
A.explain: Verbs ending in -ss, -sh, -ch, -x, -o add -es.

A.q: What is the 3rd person singular form of the verb 'watch'?
A.explain: Verbs ending in -ch add -es.

A.q: What is the 3rd person singular form of the verb 'buy'?
A.explain: Verbs ending in vowel + y simply add -s.

A.q: We do the shopping on Saturdays. → Correct question and negation:
A.explain: Subject 'we' uses Do / don't + base form.
options: Does we do the shopping on Saturdays? We doesn't do the shopping on Saturdays.
Do we do the shopping on Saturdays? We don't do the shopping on Saturdays.
Do we does the shopping on Saturdays? We don't does the shopping on Saturdays.
Are we do the shopping on Saturdays? We aren't do the shopping on Saturdays.

A.q: Which is the correct 3rd person singular of 'fix'?
A.explain: Verbs ending in -x add -es.

A.q: The news ______ (be) interesting every day. (Note: 'news' is singular)
A.explain: 'News' is an uncountable/singular noun → is.

A.q: Neither the students nor the teacher ______ gap hours.
A.explain: With 'neither...nor', the verb agrees with the closer subject (the teacher = singular).

A.q: He _________ even his own name.
A.explain: Third-person singular 'He' requires 'does not' (doesn't) + base verb.

A.q: The boy _________ his homework.
A.explain: 'The boy' is third-person singular. The negative auxiliary is 'doesn't', followed by the base form 'do'.

A.q: The girls _________ to go.
A.explain: 'The girls' is plural, requiring 'don't' + base verb 'want'.

A.q: That boy _________ to go to school.
A.explain: 'That boy' is singular. We use 'doesn't' and the base verb 'like'.

A.q: Most children _________ math or grammar.
A.explain: 'Children' is the irregular plural of 'child'. Plural subjects take 'don't'.

A.q: Pigeons _________ make nests.
A.explain: 'Pigeons' is plural. The auxiliary 'don't' is used before the main verb 'make'.

A.q: Every boy and girl in the school _________ to go on the field trip.
A.explain: The distributive determiner 'Every' makes the compound subject singular, so 'doesn't' is required.

A.q: The news about the pigeons _________ make the farmers happy.
A.explain: 'News' is an uncountable singular noun, so it takes the singular auxiliary 'doesn't'.

A.q: Mathematics _________ seem to be liked by most children.
A.explain: 'Mathematics' is a singular field of study, so it takes 'doesn't'.

A.q: Each of the vegetarians _________ eat fish.
A.explain: The subject is the singular indefinite pronoun 'Each', so 'doesn't' is correct.

A.q: Neither the teachers nor the principal _________ know the answer.
A.explain: With 'neither...nor', the verb agrees with the subject closest to it. 'Principal' is singular and closest, so 'doesn't' is used.

A.q: The boy, along with his sisters, _________ like to go to school.
A.explain: The subject is 'The boy' (singular). The phrase 'along with his sisters' does not change the number of the subject, so 'doesn't' is correct.

A.q: He is the only one of those vegans who _________ use milk products.
A.explain: The phrase 'the only one of those vegans who' refers to the singular 'one', so 'doesn't' is used.

A.q: A large number of pigeons _________ make nests here, but the exact number of nests _________ matter to the farmer.
A.explain: 'A number of' takes a plural verb 'don't'. 'The number of' takes a singular verb 'doesn't'.

A.q: The fact that most children _________ like math or grammar _________ surprise the new teacher.
A.explain: The first blank is in a dependent clause with 'children' (plural) so 'don't'. The second blank is the main verb for 'The fact' (singular) so 'doesn't'.

A.q: Eating fish or meat _________ appeal to vegans, but avoiding dairy and eggs _________ seem to be a challenge for some.
A.explain: Gerund phrases act as singular nouns, so both blanks take 'doesn't'.

B.q: Don't/Doesn't are used to form which type of sentence in the simple present?
B.explain: Don't and doesn't are used to form negative simple present sentences.

B.q: In the structure "Subject + ___ + verb", what grammatical role do don't/doesn't play?
B.explain: don't/doesn't are auxiliary (helping) verbs; the real action stays in the main verb that follows.

B.q: What is the correct word order for a simple present negative?
B.explain: The correct order is: Subject + auxiliary (don't/doesn't) + base form of the verb.

B.q: Make negative: "He speaks English."
B.explain: He takes doesn't, and the -s is dropped from 'speaks'.

B.q: The main verb that follows don't/doesn't must be in the:
B.explain: After don't/doesn't the main verb is always base form: doesn't speak, don't like.

B.q: Which set of subject pronouns takes "doesn't"?
B.explain: doesn't = third person singular: he, she, it (and any singular noun).

B.q: Which set of subject pronouns takes "don't"?
B.explain: don't = first person (I, we), second person (you), and third person plural (they) — plus all plural subjects.

B.q: Sara and Tom ___ speak French.
B.explain: Two people joined by 'and' = they → don't.

B.q: Which is correct, and why?
options: He doesn't has a pen, because third person requires has
He doesn't have a pen, because the -s moved to does, so the main verb reverts to base form
Both are correct in different regions

B.q: The news ___ change my opinion.
B.explain: 'News' ends in -s but is uncountable/singular → it → doesn't.

B.q: Mathematics ___ make sense to me.
B.explain: School subjects in -s (mathematics, physics, economics) are singular → doesn't.

B.q: Everyone ___ know the answer.
B.explain: 'Everyone' means many people but is grammatically singular → doesn't.

B.q: One of my friends ___ speak German.
B.explain: The head noun is 'One' (singular) — 'of my friends' is just a modifier → doesn't.

B.q: Which is the standard-English way to say he never speaks English?
B.explain: 'never' already contains the negative — no don't/doesn't needed. (Alternative: 'He doesn't ever speak English.')

B.q: Choose the correct placement of 'always':
B.explain: Frequency adverbs go between the auxiliary and the main verb — and the main verb stays base form.
options: He doesn't tell always the truth.
He doesn't always tell the truth.
He doesn't always tells the truth.
He always doesn't tell the truth.

B.q: "Why ___ she come to class?"
B.explain: Wh-word + doesn't + base verb: 'Why doesn't she come to class?'

B.q: "Yesterday he ___ come to class."
B.explain: 'Yesterday' forces past tense → didn't, not doesn't.

B.q: Which correctly expresses that she is unable to swim?
B.explain: Modals (can, must, will) negate themselves: can't, mustn't, won't. They never accept do/does/don't/doesn't.

B.q: "He doesn't speak English, ___?"
B.explain: Negative statement → positive question tag, matching the auxiliary: 'does he?'

B.q: Which positive → negative correlation is correct?
B.explain: Only the third option is valid on both sides: positive has exactly one -s (likes), negative has exactly one -s (does).
options: He likes coffee → He doesn't likes coffee
He likes coffee → He don't like coffee
He likes coffee → He doesn't like coffee
He like coffee → He doesn't like coffee

B.q: I don't like coffee. ___
B.explain: To agree with a negative statement, use 'Me neither' (or 'Neither do I').

B.q: "There ___ seem to be a problem."
B.explain: 'There doesn't seem to be' — the dummy 'there' borrows agreement from the notional subject 'a problem' (singular).

B.q: "She doesn't enjoy ___ movies."
B.explain: After 'enjoy', the verb takes -ing: 'enjoy watching'. The don't/doesn't + base rule only governs the verb directly after the auxiliary.

B.q: Which statement is completely true?
B.explain: He speaks → He doesn't speak. The -s is conserved, not destroyed — it just changes address.
options: The third-person -s lives on the main verb in positives and transfers to the auxiliary (does) in negatives — exactly one -s per clause
The -s is deleted in negatives and appears nowhere
The -s must appear on both the verb and the auxiliary
The -s appears only with the subject 'I'

B.q: Only ONE sentence is fully correct. Which?
B.explain: The first has wrong agreement + double -s; the second has wrong agreement; the third has double -s. The fourth satisfies both rules at once.

B.q: Which statement about the subject "you" is TRUE?
B.explain: Second person is agreement-invisible: one friend or a whole classroom, 'you' → don't.
options: 'You' takes doesn't when it refers to one person
'You' always takes don't — whether singular or plural

B.q: "Each of the students ___ have a textbook."
B.explain: The head word is 'Each' (singular) — 'of the students' merely modifies it → doesn't.

B.q: Which sentence correctly says that both of your parents are non-smokers?
B.explain: 'Neither' already contains a negative — adding don't/doesn't creates a double negative, so the verb stays affirmative.
options: Neither of my parents don't smoke.
Neither of my parents doesn't smoke.
Both A and B are correct.

B.q: "A lot of people ___ know the answer."
B.explain: 'A lot of people' = they (plural) → don't. The quantifier 'a lot of' takes the number of the noun after it.

B.q: "The information ___ include prices."
B.explain: 'Information' is uncountable → singular → doesn't.

B.q: Which transformation breaks the One -S Law?
B.explain: The third option leaves -s on the main verb and also puts it on the auxiliary — two -s markers in one clause, which English forbids.
options: She works here → She doesn't work here

B.q: Check all seven mini-sentences: (1) I don't, (2) You don't, (3) He doesn't, (4) She doesn't, (5) It doesn't, (6) We don't, (7) They don't. How many are correct?
B.explain: The complete map: first person (I, we) → don't; second person (you) → don't; third person singular (he, she, it) → doesn't; third person plural (they) → don't.

B.q: What is the primary function of using 'Do' or 'Does' in English?
B.explain: Do or Does is used to make a question in the simple present tense.
options: To make a question in the simple present tense.

B.q: Which auxiliary verb is used with the subject group 'I / you / we / they' in simple present questions?
B.explain: The auxiliary 'Do' is used with I, you, we, they in simple present questions.

B.q: Which pronouns take the auxiliary 'Does' in simple present questions?
B.explain: The auxiliary 'Does' is used with he, she, it (and singular nouns).

B.q: Which auxiliary verb should be used with the word 'Everybody' in a simple present question?

C.q: Physical exercise benefits the brain in addition to which other part of the human system?
C.explain: Exercise increases blood flow and oxygen delivery throughout the entire body, which simultaneously improves physical fitness and cognitive brain function.

C.q: Which aspect of physical hygiene is scientifically connected to the long-term health of the brain?
C.explain: Poor oral health and gum disease are linked to systemic inflammation, which can negatively impact brain health and increase the risk of cognitive decline.

C.q: At what age or stage does the human brain's capacity for improvement and neuroplasticity stop?
C.explain: Neuroplasticity allows the brain to form new neural connections throughout a person's entire life, meaning cognitive improvement never truly has to stop.
options: It does not stop at any particular time; it can continue for life

C.q: Skimming a text means:
C.explain: Skimming gives the overview from headings, summaries, and key sentences. Scanning, not skimming, hunts for one specific detail.
options: Searching rapidly for one specific date or name
Reading rapidly for the general idea, using headings, titles, and first and last sentences

C.q: Scanning a text means:
C.explain: Scanning targets details such as numbers or names without reading everything. In Medical English a scan is instead an imaging test, a separate sense.
options: Moving the eyes rapidly to locate a specific piece of information

C.q: An early sign of Alzheimer's disease, often mistaken for normal aging, is:
C.explain: The early stage shows mild memory lapses for recent events. Severe physical signs such as paralysis appear only in later stages.
options: Memory lapses, especially for recent events

C.q: As Alzheimer's progresses, patients may struggle to find words or use language. This difficulty is called:
C.explain: Aphasia is impaired language use, including word-finding difficulty. It is distinct from memory loss itself and from sleep problems.

C.q: In the middle stages of Alzheimer's, patients often:
C.explain: The middle stage brings recognition problems and personality change beyond simple memory lapses. Recovery of memory does not occur in this disease.
options: Fail to recognize familiar people and places and show personality changes

C.q: A dangerous behavior in later stages of Alzheimer's, in which patients walk away and get lost even in familiar surroundings, is called:
C.explain: Disorientation drives wandering, a major safety risk requiring supervision. The other options name unrelated clinical actions.

C.q: In the final stage of Alzheimer's, patients may become catatonic, which involves:
C.explain: The end stage destroys motor and speech function, leaving patients rigid, unresponsive, and unable to swallow. Lucidity does not return at this stage.
options: Rigid muscles, unresponsiveness, and inability to swallow or sit unaided

C.q: Alzheimer's is described as progressive because:
C.explain: Progressive means gradually worsening, and each stage of Alzheimer's adds greater decline. It does not improve or resolve on its own.
options: Its symptoms worsen stage by stage over time
It appears only once and ends

C.q: What is the difference between acute and chronic insomnia?
C.explain: Acute episodes are brief and situational, while chronic insomnia is long-lasting and frequent. Neither form is treated with surgery.
options: Acute is short-term, often after stress or jet lag, while chronic persists over a long period

C.q: Which group lists common causes of insomnia?
C.explain: Travel, stimulants, and worry disrupt sleep onset and maintenance. The other groups name unrelated medical items and fields.
options: Jet lag, caffeine, stress, and anxiety

C.q: If you lie in bed restless and unable to sleep, the recommended response is:
C.explain: Leaving the bed breaks the link between bed and wakefulness, easing restlessness. Caffeine and bright screens worsen insomnia.
options: Get up and do a quiet, relaxing activity until sleepy

C.q: The present progressive tense is primarily used to describe actions that are:
C.explain: The present progressive tense describes actions that are currently happening or temporary situations occurring around the present moment.
options: in progress now or around the present time

C.q: Which of the following sentences is written in the present progressive tense?
C.explain: The sentence uses the auxiliary verb 'is' followed by the present participle 'thinking', which is the standard structure for the present progressive.
options: She is thinking beautiful calm thoughts.
Chemicals in blueberries improve your brain.

C.q: Which time expression is most typically used with the present progressive tense?
C.explain: Time expressions like 'right now', 'at the moment', and 'currently' signal that an action is in progress, requiring the present progressive tense.

C.q: Which time expression is not typically used with the present progressive tense?
C.explain: 'Every day' indicates a routine or habit, which requires the simple present tense rather than the present progressive.

C.q: Choose the correct verb form: Jane usually wears her watch on her right arm, but this week she ___ it on her left arm.
C.explain: The phrase 'this week' indicates a temporary deviation from a routine, which requires the present progressive tense 'is wearing'.

C.q: Choose the correct verb form: Joe usually drives to work, but this month he ___ to work every day.
C.explain: The time marker 'this month' highlights a temporary situation contrasting with his usual habit, necessitating the present progressive 'is walking'.

C.q: What is the standard grammatical structure for the present continuous tense?
C.explain: The present continuous (or progressive) is formed by combining the appropriate form of the verb 'to be' with the present participle (-ing form) of the main verb.

C.q: In the sentence 'The teacher is explaining the lesson now', which word functions as the auxiliary verb?
C.explain: The word 'is' is the auxiliary (helping) verb that works with the main verb 'explaining' to create the present progressive tense.

C.q: Which of the following is a grammatically correct negative contraction?
C.explain: The pronoun 'They' pairs with 'are', and the correct negative contraction for 'are not' is 'aren't'.

C.q: According to standard spelling rules, what is the correct -ing form of the verb 'happen'?
C.explain: Because the stress in 'happen' is on the first syllable, the final consonant is not doubled when adding -ing.

C.q: Why is the 'e' kept in the -ing form of the verb 'be' (being)?
C.explain: Unlike verbs with a silent 'e', the 'e' in 'be' and 'see' is pronounced, so it is retained when adding -ing.
options: Because it ends in a vowel
Because it is an irregular verb

C.q: In the sentence 'Swimming is fun', what grammatical role does the word 'Swimming' play?
C.explain: When a verb ending in -ing functions as the subject or object of a sentence, it is classified as a gerund, which acts as a noun.
options: It is a gerund acting as a noun
It is a present progressive verb

C.q: What is the correct word order for forming a yes/no question in the present progressive tense?
C.explain: To form a yes/no question in the present progressive, the auxiliary verb 'be' is placed at the beginning, followed by the subject and the main verb with -ing.

C.q: What is the correct short answer to the question 'Is the teacher explaining the lesson now'?
C.explain: Short answers in the present progressive use the pronoun and the auxiliary verb 'be'. 'Yes, she is' is the correct affirmative form.

C.q: Which of the following is an INCORRECT short answer to a yes/no question?
C.explain: In affirmative short answers, the pronoun and the auxiliary verb cannot be contracted. 'Yes, he's' is grammatically incorrect.

C.q: What is the correct word order for forming a Wh- question in the present progressive tense?
C.explain: Wh- questions in the present progressive start with the question word, followed by the auxiliary 'be', the subject, and the main verb ending in -ing.

C.q: In the sentence 'Ali is playing football in the backyard', what does the question 'What is Ali playing?' ask for?
C.explain: The question word 'What' is used to inquire about the direct object of the action, which in this case is 'football'.

C.q: In formal academic writing, which of the following sentences is preferred?
C.explain: Formal writing generally avoids contractions, making the full form 'is not' the most appropriate choice for academic contexts.

C.q: I ___ breakfast at 7:00 every morning.
C.explain: The pronoun 'I' takes the base form of the verb in the simple present tense to describe a daily routine.

C.q: He always ___ a suit to work.
C.explain: The third-person singular pronoun 'he' requires the verb to end in '-s' in the simple present tense.

C.q: A mechanic ___ cars for a living.
C.explain: The singular subject 'a mechanic' requires the third-person singular verb form 'fixes'.

C.q: She often ___ chicken for dinner.
C.explain: The adverb 'often' indicates a habit, requiring the simple present tense. The subject 'she' takes 'eats'.

C.q: They ___ the bus to school every day.
C.explain: The plural pronoun 'they' takes the base form of the verb 'take' in the simple present tense.

C.q: Mrs. Smith wants a divorce. She ___ her husband anymore.
C.explain: The singular subject 'she' requires 'doesn't'. 'Love' is a stative verb, making 'isn't loving' grammatically inappropriate here.

C.q: Poor people ___ a lot of money.
C.explain: The plural subject 'poor people' takes 'don't'. 'Have' indicating possession is a stative verb, so 'aren't having' is incorrect.

C.q: Jessica is very healthy. She ___ cigarettes.
C.explain: The singular subject 'she' requires the negative auxiliary 'doesn't' followed by the base verb 'smoke'.

C.q: Which is the correct yes/no question for the statement: 'He takes the bus to school.'?
C.explain: To form a yes/no question in the simple present with 'he', use the auxiliary 'does' followed by the base verb 'take'.
options: Does he take the bus to school?
Do he take the bus to school?
Does he takes the bus to school?
Is he take the bus to school?

C.q: Which is the correct yes/no question for the statement: 'They don't live in a big city.'?
C.explain: The plural subject 'they' requires the auxiliary 'do', and the main verb remains in its base form 'live'.
options: Do they live in a big city?
Does they live in a big city?
Do they lives in a big city?
Are they live in a big city?

C.q: Which is the correct yes/no question for the statement: 'The students work hard.'?
C.explain: The plural subject 'the students' takes the auxiliary 'do', and the main verb 'work' does not take an '-s'.

C.q: Which is the correct yes/no question for the statement: 'She doesn't eat in the cafeteria.'?
C.explain: The singular subject 'she' requires the auxiliary 'does', and the main verb reverts to its base form 'eat'.
options: Does she eat in the cafeteria?
Do she eat in the cafeteria?
Does she eats in the cafeteria?
Is she eat in the cafeteria?

C.q: Which is the correct yes/no question for the statement: 'I speak French.'?
C.explain: When converting a first-person statement to a second-person question, 'I' changes to 'you', which takes the auxiliary 'do'.

C.q: Statement: 'They have three children.' Which question correctly asks for the quantity of children?
C.explain: 'How many' is used for plural countable nouns, and the plural subject 'they' requires the auxiliary 'do'.
options: How many children do they have?
How many children does they have?
How much children do they have?

C.q: Statement: 'He speaks four languages.' Which question correctly asks for the number of languages?
C.explain: 'How many' is used for countable nouns. The singular subject 'he' requires the auxiliary 'does', and the main verb is 'speak'.
options: How many languages does he speak?
How many languages do he speak?
How many languages does he speaks?
How much languages does he speak?

D.q: Statement: 'She lives with her roommate.' Which question correctly asks for the person she lives with?
D.explain: In standard English questions, the auxiliary 'does' precedes the subject 'she', and the main verb remains in the base form 'live'.

D.q: Statement: 'They eat lunch in the cafeteria every day.' Which question correctly asks for the location?
D.explain: 'Where' asks for a place. The plural subject 'they' requires the auxiliary 'do' before the subject.
options: Where do they eat lunch every day?
Where they eat lunch every day?
Where does they eat lunch every day?
When do they eat lunch every day?

D.q: Statement: 'She doesn't want to go to a movie because she is very tired.' Which question correctly asks for the reason?
D.explain: 'Why' asks for a reason. The negative auxiliary 'doesn't' precedes the singular subject 'she', followed by the base verb 'want'.
options: Why doesn't she want to go to a movie?
Why doesn't she wants to go to a movie?
Why she doesn't want to go to a movie?
Why don't she want to go to a movie?

D.q: I never ___ coffee before I go to bed.
D.explain: Frequency adverbs like 'never' are placed before the main verb. The pronoun 'I' takes the base form 'drink'.

D.q: She always ___ her mother with the housework.
D.explain: The adverb 'always' precedes the main verb. The singular subject 'she' requires the third-person singular form 'helps'.

D.q: Her husband never ___ the laundry.
D.explain: The adverb 'never' provides the negative meaning, so the affirmative auxiliary 'does' is used with the singular subject 'her husband'.

D.q: It often ___ in April.
D.explain: The dummy subject 'it' referring to weather takes the third-person singular verb 'rains' in the simple present.

D.q: Which sentence uses the frequency adverb 'seldom' correctly?
D.explain: Frequency adverbs are placed before the main verb. The singular subject 'he' requires the verb 'drinks'.

D.q: It is a beautiful day. The sun ___ .
D.explain: The present continuous tense is used for actions happening at the moment of speaking, formed with 'is' + 'shining'.

D.q: Mother is busy now. She ___ dinner.
D.explain: The time marker 'now' indicates an action in progress, requiring the present continuous form 'is making'.

D.q: You should take your umbrella. It ___ .
D.explain: The current weather condition is described using the present continuous tense 'is raining'.

D.q: Anna is going to a wedding. She ___ a beautiful dress.
D.explain: The action of wearing the dress is happening currently for the event, requiring the present continuous 'is wearing'.

D.q: The students are in the library. They ___ .
D.explain: The plural subject 'they' combined with an ongoing action requires the present continuous form 'are reading'.

D.q: Peter ___ mathematics, but he ___ history.
D.explain: Stative verbs like 'like' are used in the simple present. The singular subject 'Peter' takes 'likes' and the negative 'doesn't like'.

D.q: She ___ a letter to her grandmother, but she ___ a letter to her aunt.
D.explain: The singular subject 'she' requires 'writes' in the affirmative and 'doesn't write' in the negative simple present.

D.q: We ___ a new car; we ___ a used car.
D.explain: The plural subject 'we' takes 'have'. 'Have' indicating possession is stative, so 'aren't having' is incorrect.

D.q: He usually ___ the bus, but today he ___ a taxi.
D.explain: 'Usually' indicates a routine (simple present 'takes'), while 'today' indicates a temporary action (present continuous 'is taking').

D.q: She ___ she doesn't like coffee, but right now she ___ tea.
D.explain: 'Says' expresses a general statement or opinion (simple present), while 'right now' requires the present continuous 'is drinking'.

D.q: My brother ___ video games every night, but he ___ TV now.
D.explain: 'Every night' signals a habit (simple present 'plays'), whereas 'now' signals an ongoing action (present continuous 'is watching').

D.q: The teacher ___ three languages, but right now she ___ English.
D.explain: Language ability is a general fact (simple present 'speaks'), while the current action is temporary (present continuous 'is speaking').

D.q: I ___ what you mean, but I ___ about something else right now.
D.explain: 'Understand' is a stative verb and remains in the simple present. 'Think' as a mental process happening 'right now' takes the present continuous.

D.q: He ___ a suit to work, but today he ___ jeans.
D.explain: General habits use the simple present ('wears'), while temporary deviations happening 'today' use the present continuous ('is wearing').

D.q: We ___ dinner at 7:00, but tonight we ___ at 8:00.
D.explain: A regular schedule uses the simple present ('eat'), while a specific plan for 'tonight' uses the present continuous ('are eating').

D.q: The baby ___ in her crib now, but she usually ___ at 8:00.
D.explain: The action happening 'now' takes the present continuous ('is sleeping'), while the routine indicated by 'usually' takes the simple present ('sleeps').

D.q: You ___ to wear a coat today because it ___ .
D.explain: 'Need' is a stative verb and takes the simple present negative 'don't need'. The current weather requires the present continuous 'is raining'.

D.q: Jessica ___ cigarettes, so she ___ right now.
D.explain: A general habit uses the simple present ('doesn't smoke'), and the resulting current state uses the present continuous ('isn't smoking').

D.q: ___ she like tea?
D.explain: 'Like' is a main stative verb, so questions in the simple present require the auxiliary 'does' for the singular subject 'she'.

D.q: She ___ like tea.
D.explain: To negate a main verb like 'like' in the simple present, use the auxiliary 'doesn't' for third-person singular subjects.

D.q: ___ you usually get up early?
D.explain: The adverb 'usually' indicates a routine requiring the simple present. The subject 'you' takes the auxiliary 'do'.

D.q: ___ you getting up early tomorrow?
D.explain: The present continuous ('getting up') is used here for a future arrangement, requiring the auxiliary 'are' with the subject 'you'.

D.q: She ___ never late for class.
D.explain: With the verb 'to be', frequency adverbs like 'never' are placed after the verb. The singular subject 'she' takes 'is'.

D.q: Dad ___ us to school every morning.
D.explain: Every morning signals a routine, so the Present Simple is used. Dad is third-person singular, requiring the verb to end in -s.

D.q: Max ___ at an Internet cafe this summer.
D.explain: This summer indicates a temporary period, which naturally takes the Present Progressive. The simple present would imply a permanent job.

D.q: We ___ abroad this year because of the pandemic.
D.explain: This year refers to a specific current or future plan, requiring the negative Present Progressive. The simple present would incorrectly suggest a general habit.

D.q: It never ___ in the Atacama Desert in Chile.
D.explain: The word never combined with a general fact about climate requires the Present Simple. The progressive would incorrectly imply it is raining right now.

D.q: Marty ___ to the fitness centre on Mondays.
D.explain: On Mondays and usually signal a habit, requiring the Present Simple. The frequency adverb usually is correctly placed before the main verb in negative sentences.

D.q: What is that? - I ___ sounds that are not there.
D.explain: Hear is a stative verb of perception, so the Present Simple is used even when referring to the current moment. The progressive form is not typically used for involuntary perception.

D.q: We ___ of leaving Britain next year. We might go to America.
D.explain: The phrase think of means to consider, which is a dynamic action allowing the Present Progressive. When think means to hold an opinion, it remains in the simple present.

D.q: I ___ my ex-husband next Monday.
D.explain: Here, see means to meet, and next Monday indicates a fixed future arrangement, requiring the Present Progressive. The simple present would imply a regular schedule.

D.q: This box ___ a lot. What is in it?
D.explain: In this context, weigh means to have a specific weight, which is a stative meaning requiring the Present Simple. The progressive is only used when weigh means the action of measuring weight.

D.q: What ___ under the table? - Is there anything wrong?
D.explain: The question asks about an action happening right now, which requires the Present Progressive. The simple present would ask about a general habit or occupation.

D.q: She never ___ to anyone about her problems.
D.explain: The word never signals a habitual fact, requiring the Present Simple. The third-person singular subject she requires the verb to end in -s.

D.q: Mary ___ very sad. What's happened to her?
D.explain: When look is followed by an adjective, it means to appear or seem, which is a stative meaning requiring the Present Simple. The progressive is used for the deliberate action of looking at something.

D.q: They ___ a few days in Stockholm next month.
D.explain: Next month and a few days describe a specific future arrangement or plan, requiring the Present Progressive. The simple present would imply a regular, repeated habit.

D.q: You can't go in. They ___ a meeting.
D.explain: Having a meeting is an activity currently in progress, requiring the Present Progressive. The simple present is used when have indicates possession.

D.q: I ___ I'll have a cup of coffee. I'm so tired.
D.explain: Here, think means to believe or hold an opinion, which is a stative meaning requiring the Present Simple. The progressive would incorrectly imply the active process of considering.

D.q: ___ fishing with me on Sunday? - I don't know. I'll think about it.
D.explain: Sunday refers to a specific future arrangement or intention, requiring the Present Progressive. The simple present would ask about a regular, repeated habit.

D.q: Max ___ to be a nice student. Let's see how he ___ in class.
D.explain: Appear to be means to seem, which is a stative verb requiring the Present Simple. Asking about general performance in class also describes a routine, taking the simple present.

D.q: I ___ what this letter means. It ___ no sense.
D.explain: Understand is a stative verb and make sense describes a general fact, so both require the Present Simple. Stative verbs are rarely used in the progressive form.

D.q: ___ at night?
D.explain: The phrase ever at night asks about a general, habitual experience, requiring the Present Simple. The progressive would unusually focus on a temporary action rather than a general habit.

D.q: I ___ on you to help me organise the meeting.
D.explain: Simple present ('count') expresses general reliance, while present continuous ('am counting') emphasizes the current situation.
options: Stative 'count' and Action 'am counting' depend on the meaning

D.q: My sister ___ a video conference in her company next week.
D.explain: Next week indicates a specific future arrangement, requiring the Present Progressive. The simple present would describe a regular, scheduled event.

D.q: Why ___ to what he has to say.
D.explain: This sentence criticizes a repeated, general habit, requiring the Present Simple. The progressive would describe a temporary action rather than a character trait.

D.q: She usually ___ to work, but this week she ___ the bus because her car is broken.
D.explain: Usually indicates a habitual action taking the Present Simple, while this week describes a temporary situation requiring the Present Progressive.

D.q: He ___ about his exams. That's why he's so quiet.
D.explain: The phrase think about means to consider or ponder, which is a dynamic action in progress. When think is used to state an opinion, it takes the simple present.

D.q: I ___ you're right, but I ___ about your offer.
D.explain: The first think means to believe, which is stative and takes the Present Simple. The second think about means to consider, which is dynamic and takes the Present Progressive.

D.q: The train ___ at 6:00, so I ___ John at 5:30 at the station.
D.explain: Timetables and schedules use the Present Simple, while personal future arrangements use the Present Progressive.

D.q: This perfume ___ wonderful. Why ___ it?
D.explain: When smell means to possess a scent, it is stative and takes the Present Simple. When it means the deliberate action of sniffing, it is dynamic and takes the Present Progressive.

D.q: You ___ silly today. Usually you ___ so serious.
D.explain: The phrase be being plus an adjective describes temporary behavior happening today. The simple present describes a permanent character trait.

D.q: I ___ a headache, so I ___ a painkiller.
D.explain: "I have a headache, so I am taking a painkiller [as we speak / right now]." vs. "I have a headache, so I will take a painkiller [in a minute]."

D.q: Why ___? You ___ usually so patient.
D.explain: Complaining right now is an action in progress, taking the Present Progressive. Being usually patient describes a permanent character trait, taking the Present Simple.

D.q: I ___ on you for this event; I ___ on you generally.
D.explain: Relying on someone for a specific, immediate event uses the Present Progressive. Relying on someone generally uses the Present Simple.

D.q: She ___ happy, but she ___ at the photo.
D.explain: Looking happy describes an appearance, which is stative and takes the Present Simple. Looking at a photo is a deliberate action, taking the Present Progressive.

D.q: He ___ always ___ his keys! It's so annoying.
D.explain: Using always with the Present Progressive expresses annoyance at a repeated, irritating habit. The simple present would simply state a neutral fact.

D.q: She usually ___ about work, but today she ___ quiet.
D.explain: Usually indicates a regular habit taking the Present Simple. Today combined with a temporary behavior uses the structure be being plus an adjective.

D.q: I ___ what you mean now; earlier I ___.
D.explain: Understand is a stative verb and does not take the progressive form, even when referring to the present moment. The earlier action requires the Past Simple.

D.q: The box ___ 10 kilos. The porter ___ it now.
D.explain: When weigh means to have a specific mass, it is stative and takes the Present Simple. When it means the physical action of measuring, it takes the Present Progressive.

D.q: He ___ to be asleep, but he ___ TV under the blanket.
D.explain: Appearing to be asleep means seeming, which is stative and takes the Present Simple. Watching TV is an action currently in progress, taking the Present Progressive.

D.q: We ___ abroad this year, but we usually ___ abroad every summer.
D.explain: This year refers to a specific, temporary plan taking the Present Progressive. Usually every summer describes a regular habit taking the Present Simple.

D.q: Why ___ so rude? You ___ usually so polite.
D.explain: Being rude right now is a temporary behavior, using the progressive form of be. Being usually polite describes a permanent trait, using the simple present.

D.q: I ___ of moving house, but I ___ it's a bad idea.
D.explain: Thinking of means considering, which is a dynamic action taking the Present Progressive. Thinking that means believing, which is a stative verb taking the Present Simple.

D.q: When a dependent time clause is moved to the beginning of a sentence, how must the punctuation change?
D.explain: When a dependent time clause starts a sentence, it must be followed by a comma to separate it from the independent main clause.
options: The conjunction is removed and a comma is placed at the end.
The word order remains exactly the same without any punctuation changes.
A comma is placed after the time clause, before the main clause.
A semicolon is placed between the main clause and the time clause.

D.q: Which of the following phrases functions as a dependent time clause?
D.explain: "Before I take an exam" contains a subordinating conjunction and a subject-verb pair, but it cannot stand alone as a complete sentence, making it a dependent clause.

D.q: In the sentence "Before she eats dinner, she cooks it", which part of the sentence functions as the independent main clause?
D.explain: "She cooks it" is the independent main clause that expresses a complete thought and can stand alone, while "Before she eats dinner" is the dependent time clause.

D.q: Which of the following sentences containing a time clause is INCORRECTLY punctuated?
D.explain: When the independent main clause comes first ("I stay home"), no comma is used to separate it from the subordinate time clause ("when it rains").
options: When it rains, I stay home.
Before I take an exam, I study well.
I stay home, when it rains.
After she cooks dinner, she eats it.

D.q: Which of the following sentences is grammatically flawless but describes a logically impossible sequence of events?
D.explain: "Before she cooks dinner, she eats it" follows all grammatical rules for time clauses and punctuation, but it reverses the logical chronological order of preparing and consuming a meal.
options: Before she eats dinner, she cooks it.
After she cooks dinner, she eats it.
Before she cooks dinner, she eats it.
When she cooks dinner, she eats it.

D.q: Which pair of sentences correctly demonstrates the punctuation rules for time clauses when the order of the clauses is reversed?
D.explain: When the time clause is at the end of the sentence, no comma is needed. When it is moved to the front, a comma must separate it from the main clause.
options: "I stay home when it rains." and "When it rains I stay home."
"I stay home when it rains." and "When it rains, I stay home."
"I stay home when it rains." and "It rains when I stay home."
"When it rains, I stay home." and "I stay home, when it rains."

D.q: What is the primary definition and use of the Present Simple tense?
D.explain: The Present Simple tense is primarily used to express general truths, scientific facts, and permanent states or habits.
options: For actions happening right now at the moment of speaking.
For facts or things that are always true or generally true.
To talk about something that is happening around the time of speaking.
For temporary situations that will change soon.

D.q: Which sentence illustrates the use of the Present Continuous for an action happening right now?
D.explain: The sentence 'I am teaching an English lesson' uses the Present Continuous (am + verb-ing) to describe an action that is actively in progress at the moment of speaking.
options: It rains a lot in winter.
I am teaching an English lesson.
She goes to the gym after work.

D.q: Which of the following statements incorrectly categorizes the tense used for a given sentence?
D.explain: The sentence 'Steve is washing his hair' uses the Present Continuous to describe an action happening right now, not the Present Simple for a daily habit.
options: 'Water boils at 100 degrees' uses Present Simple because it is a general truth.
'A dog has four legs' uses Present Simple because it is a biological fact.
'Steve is washing his hair' uses Present Simple because hygiene is a daily habit.
'Whales live in the ocean' uses Present Simple because it describes their natural habitat.

D.q: Which tense is used to describe an action happening around the current time, such as reading a book over a period of days, even if not reading it at the exact moment of speaking?
D.explain: The Present Continuous is used for temporary actions or projects happening around the present period of time, even if the physical action is paused at the exact moment of speaking.

D.q: Which time expression is correctly paired with the Present Simple tense?
D.explain: Three times a month indicates a repeated frequency or habit, which correctly pairs with the Present Simple tense.

D.q: Which pair of sentences correctly contrasts a general weather fact with a temporary weather action happening now?
D.explain: 'It rains a lot in winter' is a general climatic fact requiring the Present Simple, while 'It is raining right now' is a temporary, current action requiring the Present Continuous.
options: Fact: It is raining right now. / Temporary: It rains a lot in winter.
Fact: It rains a lot in winter. / Action Now: It is raining right now.
Habit: I am living in London. / General Truth: I live in England.
Permanent: It is raining. / Temporary: It rains.

D.q: Why is the Present Continuous used in the sentence 'I am living in London at the moment' instead of the Present Simple?
D.explain: The Present Continuous emphasizes that the situation is temporary and subject to change, whereas 'I live in London' would imply a permanent residence.
options: Because moving cities requires a visa.
To indicate that the living situation is temporary rather than permanent.
Because the speaker dislikes the city.
To show that the Present Simple is better for future plans.

D.q: Which group of frequency adverbs is typically used with the Present Simple tense?
D.explain: Adverbs of frequency such as always, often, generally, sometimes, and never are standard markers for habits and routines in the Present Simple tense.
options: In the morning, afternoon, night only

D.q: How does the grammatical categorization of 'My hands are boiling' differ from the scientific fact 'Water boils at 100 degrees'?
D.explain: 'Water boils' is a scientific fact taking the Present Simple. 'My hands are boiling' uses the Present Continuous to describe a temporary, immediate physical sensation experienced right now.
options: The second sentence is invalid because only water can boil.
The second sentence uses the Present Continuous to describe a physical sensation happening at the moment of speaking, distinct from the general truth in the first sentence.
Both must use the Present Simple because they involve heat.
The second sentence describes a regular, repeated habit.

D.q: What is the grammatical result of using a Present Simple verb with the time expression 'right now' to describe an immediate action?
D.explain: The time expression 'right now' dictates the use of the Present Continuous for actions in progress. Using the Present Simple in this context violates standard grammatical rules for immediate actions.
options: It creates a grammatical error because immediate actions require the Present Continuous.
It correctly forms a sentence like 'I am eating lunch now.'
It forces the sentence into the passive voice.
Nothing changes; the Simple and Continuous tenses are interchangeable here.

D.q: Match each pronoun type to its correct function

rightItems.text: Shows who or what performs the action
Receives the action of a verb or follows a preposition
Comes before a noun to show ownership
Stands alone to show ownership and replaces a noun phrase
Refers back to the subject of the sentence

D.q: Match each pronoun set to its correct category

leftItems.text: I, you, he, she, it, we, they
me, you, him, her, it, us, them
my, your, his, her, its, our, their
mine, yours, his, hers, ours, theirs
myself, yourself, himself, herself, itself, ourselves, yourselves, themselves

Match each time connector to its meaning or time relationship
